<span class=\"quartier-margin-date\" ari: 1984In 1984, a former market-garden hall was turned into a performance venue. It became the Espace Julien — a community centre that would gradually grow into one of the most important contemporary music venues in the south of France. Not through millions spent on architects or grand cultural policies, but through the stubborn determination of people who loved music and sharing it.

2016In 2016, Marseille city council announced an “urban regeneration” project for place Jean-Jaurès. Regeneration — the word is gentle, almost neutral. What it covered was less so: a complete redevelopment of a working-class square, changes to its market, a transformation of how it was used. Some residents immediately saw what that meant in practice: the planned disappearance of what gave the neighbourhood its life, in favour of a cleaner, smoother space, more appealing to a different clientele.

2019In February 2019, the council had a 2.5-metre-high concrete wall put up around the whole square overnight. A staggeringly brutal decision — the kind of gesture that tells you everything about the relationship between an institution and the people it serves once dialogue has broken down. The market was suspended. The square vanished behind the concrete. The neighbourhood lived with that scar for months.

2023In 2023, after 39 years and some 8,000 shows, the Espace Julien changed hands. The association La Responsabilité des Rêves — born from the coming together of Le Makeda, the Théâtre de l’Œuvre, La Meson and the Espace Julien — took over the keys. The venue reopened on 22 September, with a new look and the same ambition. The story goes on.

2024In 2024, Éditions Parenthèses published Espace Julien, une aventure musicale à Marseille (Patrick Coulomb, Marie-Hélène Balivet), a book that traces those four decades through stage photos, posters and artists’ accounts. A fine book about an unlikely place that changed a city’s cultural life.

La Bataille de la Plaine, directed by Sandra Ach, Nicolas Burlaud and Thomas Hakenholz for the Primitivi collective, is a documentary shot between 2016 and 2020 that follows the struggle from the inside. La place Jean-Jaurès — que tout le monde: Place Jean-Jaurès — which everyone calls “La Plaine” — was for a long time the beating heart of the working-class neighbourhood. A market three times a week, café terraces spreading across the tarmac, old men playing pétanque, kids hanging around. An old-style square, functional, worn, alive precisely because it was not pretty.
La place a rouvert. Les travaux sont fin: The square has reopened. The works are finished. The market is back, but not quite the same. New terraces, new street furniture, a resurfaced ground. Some say it is better. Others say something is missing — that roughness, that discomfort, that freedom of use which meant the square belonged to everyone because it was not pretty for anyone in particular.
La programmation change toutes les semai: Line-ups change every week: the safest bet is to follow the venues on their websites or social media. And for before or after the gig, Le Mag has already done the rounds of the cocktail bars.
La programmation ne choisit pas son camp: The programming refuses to pick a side: rock, chanson, reggae, ska, Occitan music, electronic music, DJ sets. La programmation ne connaît pas de front: The programming knows no borders: rap, electronic, rock, and nights with a loyal following. Gâter le coin, whose takings go to an association helping unaccompanied foreign minors; Rasputin, a queer and Italo-disco collective; and the Saturday Boum, where everyone sings along to 1990s and 2000s hits.

Le Cours Julien est depuis les années 90: Since the 1990s, Cours Julien has been one of Marseille’s street art hotspots — and one of the few places in France where walls have been officially made available to artists without turning into a sanitised open-air museum. The works change, overlap, talk to each other or fade away. Some last for years, others are covered over within weeks.
Le Cours Julien tire son nom d’un ancien: Cours Julien takes its name from a former market garden that stretched across what is now the esplanade. Through the demolitions and rebuilding of the 19th and 20th centuries, the vegetable plots gave way to a dense, eclectic neighbourhood built without much of a master plan. Perhaps that is why it has kept its particular texture — streets that do not always meet at right angles, buildings that seem to have been set down almost by chance, cellars that become music venues.

Le nom dit la méthode. Au labo, on ne tr: The name says it all. In this lab, they only work with fresh ingredients, no industrial syrups. The cocktails are numbered, like formulas, and the menu includes around fifteen house mocktails, so you can finish the walk going strong.
Le nom joue sur trois tableaux&#8239;: l: The name plays on three things: the glass (verre), of course; Veracruz, the Mexican city, a nod to the Lebanese diaspora found all over the world; and Tom Cruise, the bottle-juggling bartender of the 1988 film Cocktail.
Le nom vient d’un tableau de Dalí, et il: The name comes from a Dalí painting, and it hides one of Marseille’s oldest rock bands. Leda Atomica was formed in the 1980s around Phil Spectrum, then grew into a collective with its own label, LAM. In 2001, the gang opened a workspace for all kinds of music on rue Saint-Pierre, a stone’s throw from La Plaine.
Le processus en cours dans ce quartier n: What is happening in this neighbourhood is no different from what is happening in dozens of working-class neighbourhoods across France and Europe. Rents go up. Local shops close, replaced by coffee shops and restaurants aimed at a different clientele. Families who had been here for generations leave because they can no longer afford it. New residents arrive — not necessarily bad people, not necessarily aware of what they are helping to erase.

Pendant des années, le 103 rue Ferrari s: For years, 103 rue Ferrari was called the Poste à Galène. The venue aims to be friendly, community-minded and committed, with 270 places and four nights a week.
For three years, the neighbourhood resisted. General assemblies, occupations, demonstrations, negotiations that led nowhere. A long, exhausting mobilisation, carried by people who had other things to do but cared about their square, their market, their way of living in the city.

Quartier culturel et festif de Marseille: A cultural, lively neighbourhood of Marseille, known for its bars, live music, art galleries, street art, restaurants and nightlife. In the 6th arrondissement.
Quartier populaire d’abord. Quartier de: A working-class neighbourhood first. A neighbourhood of market gardeners, craftspeople and last century’s immigrants, who brought their habits to its cafés and courtyards. Then a counterculture neighbourhood in the 1980s and 90s, when cheap rents and empty warehouses drew in artists, associations, zines and sound systems. And now — slowly, surely — a coveted neighbourhood, a neighbourhood in transformation, one whose residents sometimes watch the changes with legitimate concern.
